title: Rice for the road
hookLine: a grandmother presses rice into balls nobody will eat
carry: pinda: the living still care for the dead
tomorrow: a hard river on the road. how does anyone get across?

cards: A kitchen on a quiet morning. Rice cooling on a steel plate. Black sesame in a small bowl, a cup of water beside it.
Someone's grandmother wets her palms and presses the rice into small, firm balls, one after another, and sets them in a row. Nobody is going to eat them.
In the days after a death, families who keep the old rites make offerings like this for the one who has gone. The Garuda Purana gives a reason for them, and it may not be the reason anyone guesses.

teach.b: In the Garuda Purana's account, a person who has just died isn't on their way yet.
They're a preta, a departed one, in between, without a body to travel in.

In paraphrase, Vishnu tells Garuda that the rice-ball offerings made in the days after death build that body, piece by piece, day by day, until the departed has a form that can make the journey. Then the long road begins.
So in this picture the family isn't only grieving. They're doing something for the person they've lost: feeding them, in the text's terms, and getting them ready to go.
The rice ball is called a pinda, and it comes back in later rites too, when the departed is joined to the ancestors and remembered year after year.
Those rites are called shraddha, and they are why many Hindu families still mark the day a parent died, every year, with food, water and their name.
Some families keep the rites as the text describes them, with a priest, on the set days. Some keep a few.

teach.h: THE LIVING STILL CARE FOR THE DEAD.
teach.b: Some hear the passage as a picture of something no one can see: that the dead are still owed care, and that grief can be given work to do. The text is clear about one thing.
It puts the living and the dead in the same story, with the living doing their part. That's the first passage: a family making a body out of rice, so someone they love can travel.

how: In the days after a death, and at yearly remembrance rites (shraddha), Hindu families who keep these rites offer pindas, rice balls often mixed with sesame, usually with a priest's help; practice varies widely by family and region.

o: a Purana where Vishnu answers his eagle's questions
the priest's manual for weddings and births
a collection of eagle fables told to children

games.q: the first after-death passage — tap the pairs.
p: a rice ball offered for the departed
a body built piece by piece
the rites that remember the dead

s: in the Garuda Purana, the rice offerings are food for the mourners
they're for the departed: in the text, they build a body for the journey.
the text says a person who has just died is in between, a preta
without a body to travel in, until the offerings form one.
every Hindu family keeps these rites exactly as the text says
some keep them all, some a few, and some hear the passage as a picture.

games.q: a classmate's grandmother died last week. her family offers rice each day, and she wonders why every day instead of once. by the Garuda Purana, why?
o: it tests how devoted the family really is.
day by day, the offerings build the departed a body for the road.
it keeps the spirit from coming back to the house.
games.why: in Vishnu's answer to Garuda, the offerings form the preta's body piece by piece, until it can make the journey.

practice: Fill a cup with water. Say the name of someone you've lost, or someone far away, slowly, and pour a little of the water out, onto a plant or into the earth, in their name, the way families offer water for the departed.
If you pray, offer it to God for them. If you don't, just say the name and hold them in mind for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: The Garuda. A Purana where Vishnu tells his eagle what the living can do for the dead, starting with a ball of rice.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a ball or lump; the rice ball offered for the departed and the ancestors.

carryVoice: Your line: pinda, the living still care for the dead. A ball of rice, made by family hands. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Garuda Purana, Preta Khanda (the pinda offerings forming a body for the departed)
